name: Depression Test
tagline: Check your mood, energy and thinking over the last two weeks.
intro: Over the last two weeks, how often have you been bothered by the following problems? This screener includes the PHQ-9, a widely used depression questionnaire, plus extra questions about mood, energy, sleep, thinking and self-image. It takes about five minutes and is not a diagnosis, but it can help you understand how you are doing and whether to seek support.
seoTitle: Depression Test: Free PHQ-9 based screener
seoDescription: How has your mood been lately? Take this 5-minute depression screener with the PHQ-9 and get a personal report on mood, energy, sleep and thinking.

mood.name: Mood and enjoyment
mood.short: How often you have felt sad, empty or unable to enjoy things.
mood.low: Your answers suggest that your mood has been fairly stable over the last two weeks and that you can still enjoy things. Everyone has low moments, and that is a normal part of life. Keep doing what supports you, such as time with people you like, activities that give you joy and enough rest. Paying attention to your mood regularly helps you notice early if something changes.
mood.mid: Your answers suggest that low mood, irritability or reduced enjoyment have been bothering you on a fair number of days. This can happen during stressful periods, but it deserves attention. Try to keep doing small things you used to enjoy, even if the enthusiasm is not there yet, and share how you feel with someone you trust. If your mood does not lift within a few weeks, consider talking to your doctor.
mood.high: Your answers suggest that you have often felt down, empty or unable to enjoy things over the last two weeks. This can be very heavy, and you do not have to carry it alone. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional soon; low mood is common and treatable. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Until then, try to stay in contact with people around you.

energy.name: Energy and drive
energy.short: How tired, slowed down or unmotivated you have felt.
energy.low: Your answers suggest that your energy and drive have been reasonably good recently. You seem able to get through daily tasks and still have some energy left. Keep supporting this with regular sleep, movement and breaks. Feeling tired after a busy day is normal; it becomes a concern mainly when rest no longer seems to help. Keep an eye on how you feel during busy or stressful periods.
energy.mid: Your answers suggest that tiredness or low drive has been getting in the way on quite a few days. Daily tasks may feel heavier than usual. Try to keep a basic rhythm with regular meals, some daylight and gentle movement, which often helps more than extra rest. Break tasks into small steps. If the fatigue lasts or worsens, it is worth checking in with your doctor.
energy.high: Your answers suggest that exhaustion and low drive have been affecting you most days, making even simple tasks hard. Fatigue like this can be part of depression, but it can also have physical causes, so please talk to your doctor or a qualified professional. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Meanwhile, be gentle with yourself: lower your expectations temporarily and ask others to help with what you cannot manage right now.

sleep.name: Sleep, appetite and body
sleep.short: How much your sleep, appetite and physical wellbeing have been affected.
sleep.low: Your answers suggest that your sleep, appetite and physical wellbeing have been fairly stable recently. These basic rhythms are a strong foundation for good mood and energy. Keep protecting them with regular sleep times, balanced meals and some daily movement. Small changes are normal during stressful weeks and usually settle by themselves. If your sleep or appetite shifts for longer than a few weeks, it is worth paying closer attention.
sleep.mid: Your answers suggest that your sleep, appetite or body have been affected on a number of days. Disturbed sleep and changes in eating can both result from and add to low mood. Try to keep regular sleep and wake times, limit caffeine and alcohol in the evening and eat at fixed times, even small portions. If these problems continue, mention them to your doctor.
sleep.high: Your answers suggest that your sleep, appetite and physical wellbeing have been strongly affected over the last two weeks. These changes can be part of depression and can make everything else harder. Please discuss them with your doctor or a qualified professional, who can also check for physical causes. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Try to keep a simple routine for sleeping and eating, even when it feels difficult.

cognition.name: Thinking and concentration
cognition.short: How much your concentration, memory, decisions and thinking have been affected.
cognition.low: Your answers suggest that your concentration, memory and decision-making have been working well recently. You seem able to think clearly and keep track of things. Occasional forgetfulness or distraction is normal, especially when you are busy. Good sleep, breaks and limiting multitasking will help you keep your mind sharp. If you notice your thinking becoming slower or more negative over time, take it as a signal to slow down and check in with yourself.
cognition.mid: Your answers suggest that concentrating, deciding or thinking clearly has been harder than usual on quite a few days, and you may be stuck in worrying thoughts at times. This is a common effect of stress and low mood. Write things down, focus on one task at a time and postpone big decisions if possible. Talking your worries through with someone can loosen their grip.
cognition.high: Your answers suggest that brain fog, forgetfulness, indecision and repetitive negative thoughts have been bothering you most days. These are common features of depression and usually improve with the right support. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified professional about how you are doing. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. For now, keep tasks small and simple, and remind yourself that this way of thinking is a symptom, not the truth.

self_image.name: Self-image
self_image.short: How critical, guilty or worthless you have felt about yourself.
self_image.low: Your answers suggest that you have been relatively kind to yourself recently. You do not seem weighed down by guilt or harsh self-criticism. A balanced self-image helps you cope with setbacks and supports your mood. Keep noticing what you do well, and treat yourself with the same understanding you would offer a good friend. Self-kindness is not weakness; it makes it easier to learn from mistakes.
self_image.mid: Your answers suggest that self-doubt, guilt or a critical inner voice have been bothering you on a fair number of days. These thoughts often become louder when you are stressed or low. Try to notice them and ask whether you would judge a friend in the same way. Writing down small things that went well each day can gradually balance your view of yourself.
self_image.high: Your answers suggest that you have often felt worthless, guilty or very critical of yourself over the last two weeks. Such harsh thoughts are a common part of depression and do not reflect your real value. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional; therapy can really help with this. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Try to spend time with people who treat you with kindness.

summary: This report combines your PHQ-9 score, a widely used screening measure, with five areas that show where you have been most affected over the last two weeks. Higher scores mean more frequent problems. It is not a diagnosis; if your scores are raised, please talk to a doctor or qualified professional. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

instrument.name: PHQ-9 score
instrument.description: The PHQ-9 is a widely used, public-domain screening questionnaire for depression developed by Drs Kroenke, Spitzer and Williams. Your score from 0 to 27 indicates how severe your symptoms may be, but it is a screening tool and not a diagnosis.
